text: A DAC turns a stream of numbers into a voltage. Multibit and delta-sigma are two designs that disagree on how to rebuild the analog wave from the samples. Multibit builds each sample as one exact level. Delta-sigma approximates that level with a coarse switch running very fast, then shapes the leftover error out of the band you can hear. Two roads to the same clean output.
title: aadhar.sh: DACs

text: In a multibit DAC, an N-bit value selects one of 2^N voltages, and a resistor ladder (R-2R) sums the bits into exactly that level. A 16-bit sample picks one of 65,536 voltages. The raw output is a staircase, one flat step per sample, which an analog filter then smooths into a curve.
title: aadhar.sh: DACs

text: Multibit precision turns into cost. Every step has to land on its exact voltage, so the resistors must be matched to brutal tolerances: a 20-bit ladder wants resistors good to roughly 1 part per million. That is instrumentation hardware. Schiit's Yggdrasil runs a quad of 20-bit Analog Devices AD5791 ladders, the same parts used in MRI machines, because audio-grade chips cannot hold that line.
title: aadhar.sh: DACs

text: A delta-sigma DAC runs a 1-bit quantizer at 64 to 256 times the audio rate with a feedback loop, so the output works out to X(z) times z^-1 plus E(z) times (1 - z^-1). The (1 - z^-1) term is a high-pass filter on the quantization error: it pushes the noise up into ultrasonic frequencies, out of the band you hear, where a simple analog filter removes it. You trade amplitude precision for timing precision.
title: Delta-sigma modulation (Wikipedia)

text: Noise shaping is the heart of delta-sigma. Higher-order modulators raise the noise transfer function to (1 - z^-1) squared or cubed for a steeper tilt, pulling even more quantization noise out of the audible band. Because the quantizer is just a fast switch rather than a precise ladder, it stays cheap and very linear, and lower-bit-depth converters are easier to make highly linear.
title: Delta-sigma modulation (Wikipedia)

text: Nearly every DAC chip on the market today (ESS, AKM, Cirrus) is delta-sigma, because the coarse, fast, oversampled quantizer is cheap to integrate on-chip and posts excellent total-harmonic-distortion and signal-to-noise numbers. On steady-state measurements, modern delta-sigma generally beats multibit.
title: aadhar.sh: DACs

text: Multibit keeps a following for two honest reasons. Coarse bits are audible when nothing shapes them away, and some listeners argue the modulator's behavior on quiet passages and on the decay of notes sounds different in ways a steady-tone measurement will not capture. The measurable gap between good modern designs is tiny and often below audibility, but the preference is real to the people who hold it and hard to reduce to a single number.
title: aadhar.sh: DACs

text: The summary: multibit pays in hardware to make every level physically exact, while delta-sigma pays in cleverness to make the errors inaudible. Both arrive at clean sound by opposite routes; they just disagree about where to put the hard part. Quantization noise is audible at low bit depth, and delta-sigma's move is to keep the bit depth low but shove that noise above 20 kHz.
title: aadhar.sh: DACs

text: An R-2R resistor ladder turns N bits into one voltage using only two resistor values, R and 2R, one rung per bit. From any rung, the resistance looking back toward the smaller bits always works out to R, so each rung halves the contribution of the one above it: the most significant bit lands Vref/2 at the output, the next Vref/4, then Vref/8, and so on. Adding up whichever bits are switched to Vref gives Vref times the binary value divided by 2^N, all from two resistor values repeated.
title: aadhar.sh: DACs

text: In an R-2R ladder each bit's resistor sets that bit's weight, so an error in a high bit shifts the output a lot while an error in a low bit barely matters. A large enough error makes the converter non-monotonic, meaning a higher input code can produce a lower output voltage. To stay monotonic and linear, a 20-bit ladder needs resistors matched to about 1 part per million, because the most significant bit's accuracy has to beat the size of the smallest step.
title: aadhar.sh: DACs

text: A DAC's raw output is a staircase (multibit) or a fast 1-bit stream (delta-sigma), and a reconstruction filter smooths it into the analog wave by removing the spectral images above the audio band. This filter is a time-versus-frequency tradeoff: a sharp, fast filter kills the images cleanly but rings in time, while a slow filter rings less but rolls off some treble and lets a little imaging through. A non-oversampling (NOS) DAC skips the filter, so there is no ringing but the images leak through; oversampling first pushes the images far up in frequency so a gentle filter can finish the job. Filter choice is also where Schiit's Mike Moffat differs, shipping a custom closed-form filter instead of the stock windowed-sinc.
title: aadhar.sh: DACs

text: A reconstruction filter (anti-imaging filter) is a low-pass filter applied after a DAC to remove the spectral images that sampling creates, leaving the original baseband signal. The ideal reconstruction filter is a sinc function, a perfect brick-wall low-pass, but it is not physically realizable because it is infinitely long in time. Real filters therefore approximate it and trade off passband flatness, stopband sharpness, and time-domain ringing, which is a direct consequence of the Fourier relationship between a signal's width in time and in frequency.
title: Reconstruction filter (Wikipedia)
